parts.title: Enquiring about a nursery place
parts.context: A father phones a nursery to ask about a place for his daughter.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a father phoning a nursery to ask about a place for his daughter. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Little Acorns Nursery, Ms Dunne speaking.

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: Good morning. I'm calling about a nursery place for my daughter. We've just moved to the area.

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Welcome. I'd be happy to help. I'll take a few details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The place is for his daughter, so 'daughter' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: Tariq Mahmood. That's M-A-H-M-O-O-D.

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Thank you, Mr Mahmood. And your daughter's name?

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: Amira. A-M-I-R-A.

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: How old is she?

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: She's two. She'll be three in December, but we'd like her to start now.

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: That's fine. We take children from two years old. When would you like her to start?

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: As soon as possible. Would the second of September be possible?

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Yes, there is a place from then. And how many days a week would you need?

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: Three days, because my wife and I both work part-time. We thought Monday to Wednesday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Let me explain our sessions. We have three kinds. The morning session runs from eight o'clock until twelve, and it's twenty-two pounds.

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: And in the afternoon?

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: The afternoon session starts at one o'clock and finishes at six, and it costs eighteen pounds. It's cheaper because there's no meal.

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: I see. Is there an option for the whole day?

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Yes, the full day is from eight until six, and it's thirty-five pounds. That includes lunch, which is cooked fresh in our kitchen, and an afternoon snack.

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: That would suit us best, since both of us finish work late. Can we visit first?

script.speaker: dunne
script.text: Of course. Visits are on Thursday mornings, and you're welcome to bring Amira. We'll show you the rooms and the garden.

script.speaker: tariq
script.text: Thank you. I'll come on Thursday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A charity bookshop
parts.context: The manager of a charity bookshop explains the volunteer roles.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a charity bookshop talking to new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: Welcome, everyone, and thank you for volunteering at the Harbour Bookshop. I'm Liz Gordon, the manager. Let me explain how the week is organised, because each job has its own day.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: Sorting donations is on Monday mornings. That's when the weekend's bags of books are opened, and it's a big job, so we need four people for it.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: Once the books have been sorted, they need to be priced. That's done on Wednesdays, using a price guide. You'd be surprised how many books are worth more than they look.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: The window displays are changed on Thursday mornings. If you're creative, this is the job for you. The theme changes each month.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: Our online sales are handled on Tuesday afternoons. We list the more valuable books on the internet, which brings in nearly a third of our income.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: And on Saturdays, when the shop is busiest, we need people to work at the till, and chat with the customers. We're closed on Sundays, so there's no volunteering then.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: A few more details. The shop raises money for a charity that supports homeless people, with hostels and a free meal service. Everything we earn, after paying for the rent and the electricity, goes to the charity.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: On a normal day, we need four volunteers in the shop. That's enough to keep things running smoothly, but if you can't come, please let me know the day before.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: You don't need any special qualifications. All new volunteers have an informal interview with me, which is really just a conversation about what you'd like to do, and what you're good at.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: A word about the books themselves. Volunteers receive a thirty percent discount on anything they buy, but nobody can take items home before they've been priced, to keep things fair.

script.speaker: gordon
script.text: And to say thank you, every December we hold a dinner for all the volunteers, which is paid for by a local restaurant. Now, let me show you round.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A report on a lunar eclipse
parts.context: Two astronomy students write up their observation of a lunar eclipse.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two astronomy students, Hugo and Ayesha, discussing their report on a lunar eclipse. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: Ayesha, did you manage to photograph the eclipse last night? I couldn't see anything. It was completely cloudy here.

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: It was clear for the first hour, and I got some good pictures before the clouds came.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: Lucky you. What equipment did you use?

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: My phone on a tripod, and my brother's binoculars. I'd borrowed a telescope from the department, but the battery for its motor was flat.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: What time did the eclipse become total?

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: At eleven fifty, and it lasted about an hour, which is quite long.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: What colour did the moon turn?

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: Darker than I expected, a deep orange rather than bright red. I think there was a lot of dust in the atmosphere.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: Our tutor wants us to compare our photographs with the predictions.

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: I did that this morning. The prediction was within two minutes of what I saw, which is impressive.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: Now the explanation section. I'll draft it. A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth moves between the sun and the moon.

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: Right, so the moon passes into the Earth's shadow, and you'd expect it to go completely dark.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: But it doesn't, because some of the sunlight is bent by the Earth's atmosphere, and still reaches the moon.

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: And that light is mainly red, because the blue light is scattered away. It's the same reason that sunsets are red.

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: That's a nice link. Then the moon's orbit carries it out of the shadow again, and the eclipse ends.

script.speaker: ayesha
script.text: Shall we add a diagram?

script.speaker: hugo
script.text: Yes, I'll draw one this evening. You write the observations section.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of chocolate
parts.context: A history lecture on chocolate, from the Maya to milk chocolate.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of chocolate. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Chocolate is one of the world's favourite foods, yet for most of its history it was not sweet, and it was not eaten. It was a drink, and a bitter one.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Cacao trees grow naturally in the tropical forests of Central and South America. The first people to turn the beans into a drink were probably the peoples of Mesoamerica, and by the time of the Maya and the Aztecs, it was an important part of life. They prepared it with water, and flavoured it with chilli and other spices. It was frothy, and quite different from the hot chocolate we know.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The beans were so valuable that they were also used as money. Records show that a rabbit could be bought for ten beans, and a day's work paid in a small handful.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The Spanish brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century. They didn't like the bitter taste, so they added sugar, and sometimes honey and cinnamon, and the sweet drink became fashionable at the royal courts. For two centuries, it remained a luxury for the rich.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The industrial age transformed it. In eighteen twenty-eight, a Dutch chemist called Van Houten invented a press that squeezed the fat out of the beans, and produced cocoa powder, which was cheaper, and mixed more easily with water. Then in eighteen forty-seven, the English firm of Fry made the first solid bar of eating chocolate.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The next step was milk chocolate. In eighteen seventy-five, a Swiss chocolate maker named Daniel Peter combined cocoa with condensed milk, with the help of his neighbour, Henri Nestlé, who made milk products. The result was smoother and sweeter, and it made chocolate popular with children.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today, most cacao is grown in West Africa, by millions of small farmers, many of whom earn very little. There are serious concerns about child labour on some farms, and that is why fair-trade and certification schemes have become so important. Next week we'll look at the history of coffee.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
